kp.k: Mid-tier firms face an hourglass market squeeze
kp.d: Drummond argues that UK mid-tier law firms are losing traditional market share from both directions: larger firms are moving into mid-tier work, while smaller and newly structured entrants are competing from below. He characterises the resulting legal-services market as increasingly hourglass-shaped, with the middle under sustained pressure.
qs: At the other end of the law firm spectrum, new entrants with new fee/cost/earnings regimes, different management, ownership/investor structures, are coming into the Legal market and capturing market share from the mid-tier from the bottom.
Hence the ever evolving hourglass effect with market share eroding the mid-tier from the bottom as well as the top.
There is no doubt that market pressures from above and below are exacerbating the hourglass effect on the mid tier market.

kp.k: Large firms expand downward through scale and technology
kp.d: The author attributes the growing power of the Silver Circle, Magic Circle and Transatlantic Elite to deregulation, globalisation and technology. Their greater resources are said to support broader offerings, lower costs and lighter versions of global services, enabling them to encroach on work historically handled by mid-tier firms.
qs: Deregulation, globalisation and technology (Wilkinson) continue to lend greater power to the Silver Circle, Magic Circle and Transatlantic Elite.
These large firms are becoming larger and continue to encroach upon the ‘traditional’ mid-tier territory.
Greater resources allow for a greater breath of offering, reduced costs and the ability to offer global ’lite’ services, not previously identifiable with the top tier of international firms.

kp.k: New entrants compete through alternative business structures
kp.d: Drummond identifies entrants with different fee, cost, earnings, management, ownership and investor arrangements as a source of competition. The claim concerns structural innovation in legal-service provision rather than AI specifically, although embracing technology later appears among his recommendations for profitable mid-tier firms.
qs: At the other end of the law firm spectrum, new entrants with new fee/cost/earnings regimes, different management, ownership/investor structures, are coming into the Legal market and capturing market share from the mid-tier from the bottom.
- Embrace technology

kp.k: Accounting consolidation provides the author’s market analogy
kp.d: Drawing on Barry Wilkinson’s account, Drummond compares legal-market restructuring with the accounting sector’s consolidation from the Big 8 to the Big 4. The reported mechanism combines mergers, expansion into trusted-adviser and consulting roles, broader expertise, reduced fees and movement from large-corporate work into the SME market.
qs: Barry Wilkinson in his article ‘Beyond ABS – A Review of the Post Legal Services Act Market’ observes how we saw this in the accountancy world when the Big 8 became the Big 4.
Mergers were the order of the day; the big firms got considerably bigger and the mid tier became much more competitive and aspirational.

The big 4 all rebranded to become international consultancies with a broadened palette of expertise, and whilst they occupy the large corporate space, they are actively encroaching on the mid tier for more SME business.
So in the Legal sector we are beginning to see the same.

kp.k: Mergers promise scale but frequently disappoint
kp.d: The author reports mergers as the historical response to pressure on mid-tier firms, with anticipated benefits including growth, scale, geographic reach, broader expertise and cost savings. However, citing Jomati Consulting, he reports that approximately half of consulted firms would consider merging, two thirds of discussions fail, 43% of mergers are deemed successful and 21% unsuccessful.
qs: Historically a merger has seemed the elixir for mid tier firms to withstand these hourglass pressures from above and below.

The upsides were multifarious; growth, market share, economies of scale, new offices in new geographies, new areas/consolidation of expertise, broadened service offerings, cost savings – surely bigger is better in the new post LSA world?
Not necessarily so.

Recent research by Jomati Consulting has identified that although approximately half of the mid-tier firms spoken to would consider merging, two thirds of merger discussions prove ultimately unsuccessful.
Furthermore, only 43% of mergers are deemed ‘successful’ and damningly 21% of mergers ‘unsuccessful’.

kp.k: Reported merger activity fell sharply by 2016
kp.d: Using figures attributed to Jomati Consulting/Mergerline, the article reports fluctuating and then declining merger counts involving Lawyer 100 firms: 21 in 2011, 26 in 2012, 28 in 2013, 19 in 2014, 13 in 2015 and two by July 2016. The article does not establish why the count declined.
qs: In 2011 we saw 21 mergers involving law firms in the Lawyer 100, 26 mergers in 2012, 28 mergers in 2013, 19 mergers in 2014, 13 mergers in 2015 and just 2 mergers so far in 2016 (Jomati Consulting/Mergerline).

kp.k: Profitability depends on service, management, specialization, and agility
kp.d: Based on the author’s stated experience with numerous mid-tier firms, highly profitable firms are distinguished by client service, business development, firm-wide relationships, strong management and financial stewardship, strategic recruitment, agility, specialist expertise, clear positioning, competitive remuneration and fees, and technology adoption. This is presented as practitioner experience rather than a quantified study.
qs: In our experience of working with a large number of mid tier firms, the features which distinguish the highly profitable from the less so are:
- Excellent client service & delivery
- Strong management teams providing clear vision & strategy/direction and strong financial stewardship
- Agility/dynamism – able to respond to growth and change
- Specialist expertise (market sector or technical expertise)
- Clear market positioning and branding
- Embrace technology

kp.k: Adaptation and specialization matter more than maximum size
kp.d: Drummond recommends that mid-tier firms respond quickly to market demand while retaining the internal capacity to manage growth and change. His concluding prediction is conditional: firms prepared to adapt, specialise and price appropriately can flourish without becoming the largest providers.
qs: It is possible however to survive and indeed thrive.

So, to operate and grow within the post LSA, post Jackson and post recessionary market mid tier firms need to be agile, and dynamic – but able to manage growth and change internally as well as respond to market demands quickly by being prepared to specialise, at the right price.
For the squeezed middle, those firms that are prepared to adapt and specialise will be the ones who flourish.
They won’t be the biggest, but they may become the best.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The document makes no explicit claims or predictions about AI.
pts.d: Edward Drummond discusses competition and adaptation in the UK legal market, identifying technology generally alongside deregulation and globalisation as forces strengthening large firms. He also recommends that mid-tier firms embrace technology, but specifies no AI applications, capabilities or effects. These general technology references should not be treated as AI claims. The source's 'hourglass' describes a market with a squeezed mid-tier, not a firm's staffing structure.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.d: For the broader market argument, the article references Barry Wilkinson's accountancy-sector analogy, reports Jomati Consulting merger statistics, and draws on the author's organisation's experience with mid-tier firms. None of these is presented as evidence about AI's effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI adoption timeframe or conditions are stated.
pts.d: Published on July 14, 2016, the article situates its broader market analysis after the Legal Services Act, Jackson reforms and recession. Its conditional prediction concerns firms adapting and specialising, not adopting AI, and has no specified future deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No group is identified as affected specifically by AI.
pts.d: The broader discussion concerns UK mid-tier law firms losing market share to larger firms and smaller new entrants, particularly in SME business. Drummond presents agility, specialisation, competitive pricing and organisational capabilities as responses to this competition; he does not attribute the competitive pressure or these responses specifically to AI.
